unit.title: Perform head, neck and shoulder massage

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is one main benefit of a head, neck and shoulder massage?
options: It removes the need for a doctor if the client has a fever
It relaxes tight muscles and helps relieve stress and tension
It makes the hair grow back on bald patches within a week
It burns fat from the neck and shoulders to slim them down

questions.stem: How does massage affect the blood circulation in the area being worked on?
options: It increases the blood flow, bringing more oxygen to the area
It stops the blood flow, so that the muscles can rest fully
It thickens the blood, so that it moves more slowly
It has no effect on the blood, only on the skin surface

questions.stem: Why might a client feel calmer after a head, neck and shoulder massage?
options: Gentle, rhythmic movements soothe the nerves and help her relax
The oil used goes straight into the brain and makes her sleep
The massage lowers her body heat so much that she feels tired
The therapist presses on her throat to slow her breathing down

questions.stem: Which large muscle covers the back of the neck and the top of the shoulders?
options: Deltoid
Frontalis
Masseter
Trapezius

questions.stem: Where is the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: On each side of the neck, from behind the ear to the collarbone
Across the forehead, just above the eyebrows, under the hairline
Over the top of each shoulder joint, where it meets the upper arm
Down the middle of the back, along the spine

questions.stem: What is the main job of the deltoid muscle?
options: To turn and bend the head to the side
To raise the eyebrows and wrinkle the forehead
To lift the arm out to the side and forward
To close the jaw when the client is chewing

questions.stem: Which muscle raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead?
options: Occipitalis
Temporalis
Trapezius
Frontalis

questions.stem: How many bones (vertebrae) make up the neck?
options: 7 cervical vertebrae
5 cervical vertebrae
12 cervical vertebrae
24 cervical vertebrae

questions.stem: What is the everyday name for the clavicle?
options: Shoulder blade
Collarbone
Breastbone
Upper arm bone

questions.stem: What is the scapula?
options: The bone that forms the forehead
The flat, triangular shoulder blade
The first bone at the top of the neck
The bone at the back of the skull

questions.stem: Which bone forms the back and base of the skull?
options: Frontal bone
Parietal bone
Occipital bone
Temporal bone

questions.stem: Why should you avoid pressing on the front and sides of the throat?
options: The skin there is too thick for massage to have any effect
Major blood vessels and the windpipe lie close to the surface
The muscles there are too small to need any massage at all
Pressing there makes the shoulders tense up straight away

questions.stem: When massaging the upper back, why should you work on either side of the spine and not directly on it?
options: Pressure on the bones of the spine can cause pain or injury
The spine has no muscles, so massage there does nothing at all
The spine is where all the oil collects and makes it slippery
Massage on the spine will always make the client fall asleep

questions.stem: A client has a high temperature and feels unwell. What should you do?
options: Give the massage, as it will help her sweat out the fever
Give a shorter massage with extra oil to cool her down
Do not massage, and advise her to rest and see a doctor
Give a firm massage to boost her circulation and energy

questions.stem: A client was in a car accident last week and has a whiplash injury to her neck. What should you do?
options: Massage gently around the neck to ease the stiffness
Do not massage the area, and refer her to her doctor
Use very firm pressure to loosen the injured muscles
Massage the shoulders only, but twice as long as usual

questions.stem: Which of these clients needs her doctor's approval before a massage?
options: A client who is tired after a long week at work
A client with slightly dry skin on her shoulders
A client who has tight shoulders from driving
A client being treated for high blood pressure

questions.stem: A client has a small cut and some bruising on one shoulder. What should you do?
options: Avoid that area completely and work only where the skin is healthy
Put extra oil on the cut and bruise so that the massage does not sting
Massage firmly over the bruise to help it go away faster
Cover the cut with your hand and massage over it gently

questions.stem: Why should you not give a massage to a client who has just eaten a large meal?
options: The massage will make the client feel hungry again very quickly
The food will make the oil soak into the skin too fast
The client will be too heavy to sit in the chair safely
The client may feel sick or uncomfortable during the massage

questions.stem: A client arrives smelling strongly of alcohol. What should you do?
options: Give a gentle massage to help her sober up
Give the massage but leave out the neck area
Politely refuse the massage and offer to rebook
Ask her to drink coffee and then start straight away

questions.stem: What is a 'contra-action'?
options: An unwanted reaction that happens during or after a treatment
A condition that means the treatment should not be given
A massage movement that is done in the opposite direction
The consent form the client signs to agree to the treatment

questions.stem: Why do you ask about allergies before a massage with oil?
options: So that you can charge more for the oils the client likes
So that the oil can be warmed to the right temperature
Some clients react to some oils, such as nut-based oils
So that you know how much oil to pour into the bowl

questions.stem: How should the client be positioned for a seated head, neck and shoulder massage?
options: Leaning far back in the chair with her head hanging over the top
Standing up with her arms crossed tightly over her chest
Sitting on the edge of the chair with her legs crossed
Sitting upright, back supported, feet flat and arms relaxed

questions.stem: Which room setting is best for a relaxing massage?
options: Warm, quiet and private, with soft lighting
Cold and bright, next to the busy reception
Loud music, with the door open to the street
Beside the hood dryers so you can watch clients

questions.stem: Why should the client take off her earrings and necklace before the massage?
options: So that the therapist can check whether they are real
So that they can be cleaned with the massage oil
So that they do not get in the way or get damaged
So that the client does not feel too hot during it

questions.stem: Why should a massage therapist keep her nails short and her hands free of rings?
options: So that the oil does not stain the rings or the nail colour
So that she does not scratch the client or catch her hair
So that she can work faster and see more clients in a day
So that the client can see that she is not married

questions.stem: What is the hygienic way to use massage oil from a large bottle?
options: Dip your oily fingers straight into the bottle as you need it
Share one small bowl of oil between all the day's clients
Pour a small amount into a clean bowl for this client only
Leave the bottle open beside the client so it stays warm

questions.stem: Why do you warm the oil in your hands before you put it on the client?
options: To make the oil thinner so that it sinks into the bones
To mix the oil with your own skin oils so it glides better
To check that the oil has not gone off before using it
So that the client is not startled by cold oil on her skin

questions.stem: What is effleurage?
options: A deep kneading movement that lifts and squeezes the muscle
A smooth stroking movement used to begin and end the massage
A quick tapping movement done with the sides of the hands
A shaking movement done with the fingertips pressed down

questions.stem: What is the main effect of petrissage (kneading)?
options: It cools the skin and closes the pores of the shoulders
It wakes the client up with quick, light, sharp taps
It spreads the oil evenly in light, long, gliding strokes
It loosens tight muscles and helps move waste out of them

questions.stem: Tapotement is a quick, light, striking movement. What is its effect?
options: It deeply relaxes the client and slowly sends her to sleep
It stimulates and wakes up the skin, nerves and muscles
It removes all the knots in the muscles in one go
It slows the heart rate and lowers the body heat

questions.stem: Where should tapotement NOT be used?
options: Over bony areas, such as the spine and collarbones
Over the fleshy, well-padded tops of the shoulders
Over the large, thick muscles across the upper back
Over the upper arms, where there is muscle

questions.stem: What are friction movements in massage?
options: Long, light strokes over the whole of the back
Small, deep circles with the thumbs or finger pads
Fast tapping with the sides of loose, relaxed hands
Lifting and rolling the skin between the fingers

questions.stem: What is vibration in massage?
options: A firm squeeze of the muscle that is held for a whole minute
A long, gliding stroke from the neck to the shoulders
A deep kneading movement using the heels of the hands
A fine, trembling movement made with the fingers or hands

questions.stem: How should you decide how much pressure to use?
options: Use the firmest pressure you can, as deeper is always better
Start gently, ask the client, and adjust to suit her comfort
Use the same pressure for every client, whatever their size
Use light pressure only, because firm pressure is never safe

questions.stem: Why should the massage movements be smooth and rhythmic?
options: So that the massage can be finished in half the time
So that the oil does not drip onto the client's clothes
So that the client feels secure and is able to relax
So that the therapist can talk on the phone while working

questions.stem: Which posture helps the therapist work without straining her own body?
options: Bending forward from the waist with the knees locked
Feet apart, knees soft, using body weight, not just thumbs
Standing on one leg and leaning against the client's chair
Sitting very low, with the arms reaching up high

questions.stem: Why should you keep one hand in contact with the client during the massage, where you can?
options: So that the client cannot get up and leave the chair early
So that you can feel whether the room has become too warm
So that the oil does not dry out on your other hand
So that the massage feels continuous and she stays relaxed

questions.stem: Which movement is used on the scalp during a head massage?
options: Hard slapping with the palms of both hands
Pulling the hair firmly upwards in long strands
Small circular movements with the finger pads
Scratching the scalp lightly with the nails

questions.stem: Why should you tell the client what to expect before you start the massage?
options: So that she understands, can relax and can say if anything hurts
So that she knows which oils cost the most money in the salon
So that she can time each movement on her phone as you go
So that she can tell her friends how the massage is done

questions.stem: During the massage, the client says she feels dizzy. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as dizziness always passes after a few minutes
Speed up the massage so that you finish more quickly
Stop, keep her seated, and give her a glass of water
Ask her to stand up and walk around the salon quickly

questions.stem: Which aftercare advice should you give after a head, neck and shoulder massage?
options: Do some heavy weightlifting at the gym later today
Have a large meal and a few alcoholic drinks soon after
Go straight back to a stressful task without a break
Drink water, rest a little and avoid alcohol for a while

questions.stem: Which of these is a normal, mild reaction after a massage that usually passes quickly?
options: A high fever that lasts for several days
A spreading rash with blisters
Feeling tired or a little light-headed
Losing feeling in both arms

questions.stem: Why should you record the massage on the client's record card?
options: So that the client can be charged twice for the oils used
So that the therapist can give the same pressure to everyone
So that the salon can share the details with other clients
So that the next treatment can build on what was done and noted

questions.stem: After the massage, what should you do with the towels and the chair?
options: Put towels in the laundry and wipe the chair with disinfectant
Fold the towels for the next client and leave the chair oily
Shake out the towels and hang them over the chair to dry
Leave everything as it is until the end of the working day

questions.stem: When should the therapist wash her hands?
options: Before and after every massage
Only at the end of the working day
Only if her hands look dirty
Only after using oil, not cream

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: How many bones make up the cranium (the part of the skull around the brain)?
What is the name of the pair of bones that form the top and upper sides of the skull?
Which muscle at the back of the head pulls the scalp backwards?
Which fan-shaped muscle at the side of the head, over the temple, helps close the jaw when chewing?
What are the main arteries in the neck called, which carry blood from the heart to the head?

What is the name of the long bone of the upper arm, which joins the shoulder?

What is the name of the tapotement movement done with hollow, cupped hands, which makes a soft popping sound?
What is the everyday word for a tight, tender lump in a muscle, often felt across the shoulders?
What form does the client sign before the massage to show she has given her health details and agrees to the treatment?

essays.stem: Explain the benefits of a head, neck and shoulder massage for the body and for the mind.
essays.modelAnswer: For the body, massage increases the blood flow to the head, neck and shoulders, bringing more oxygen and food to the skin and muscles. It helps the lymph carry waste away, which can reduce puffiness. It warms and loosens tight muscles, such as the trapezius, which often get tense from sitting at a desk, driving or carrying heavy bags, and it can ease stiffness and tension headaches. Massage of the scalp brings blood to the hair follicles and leaves the scalp feeling fresh. The skin is softened, especially when oil is used. For the mind, the slow, rhythmic movements soothe the nerves, so the client feels calm and relaxed. It can reduce stress and worry, help the client sleep better, and lift her mood. Many clients also feel more alert and able to concentrate after a massage.
markingPoints: Increases blood flow, bringing oxygen and food to the area
Helps lymph carry waste away
Loosens tight muscles and eases stiffness or tension headaches
Calms the nerves, relaxes and reduces stress
Gives a further benefit, such as better sleep, mood or concentration

essays.stem: Describe the main muscles and bones of the head, neck and shoulders that you work on during the massage, and say where each one is.
essays.modelAnswer: The cranium is the part of the skull around the brain. It includes the frontal bone at the forehead, the two parietal bones on the top and upper sides, the two temporal bones at the sides above the ears, and the occipital bone at the back and base. The neck has seven cervical vertebrae. The shoulder is formed by the clavicle (collarbone) at the front, the scapula (shoulder blade) at the back, and the top of the humerus. The main muscles are the frontalis across the forehead and the occipitalis at the back of the head, which move the scalp. The temporalis is at the side of the head. The sternocleidomastoid runs down each side of the neck and turns the head. The large trapezius covers the back of the neck and the top of the shoulders and upper back, and lifts the shoulders. The deltoid covers the shoulder joint and lifts the arm.
markingPoints: Names and places the bones of the cranium correctly
Seven cervical vertebrae in the neck
Clavicle, scapula and humerus at the shoulder
Frontalis, occipitalis or temporalis, and sternocleidomastoid, placed correctly
Trapezius and deltoid, placed correctly, with what they do

essays.stem: Name five contraindications to a head, neck and shoulder massage and explain what you would do for each.
essays.modelAnswer: A fever or high temperature: do not massage, as it could make the client feel worse; advise rest and a doctor if needed. An infection of the skin or scalp, such as ringworm or impetigo: do not massage, because it can spread to others and to me; refer her to a doctor. A recent injury or operation on the head, neck or shoulders, such as whiplash: do not massage the area; she needs her doctor's approval first. A medical condition such as high or low blood pressure, a heart problem, epilepsy or a blood clot: do not go ahead without her doctor's approval, and follow any advice given. Cuts, bruises or swelling in one small area: avoid that area and work only on healthy skin. A client who has drunk alcohol or just eaten a large meal: rebook her. For each case I explain kindly and privately, I do not diagnose, and I record what was decided.
markingPoints: Names five sensible contraindications
Does not massage, and refers to a doctor, for fever, infection or recent injury
Asks for the doctor's approval for medical conditions such as blood pressure, heart problems or epilepsy
Avoids small local areas such as cuts or bruises, and rebooks after alcohol or a heavy meal
Explains kindly without diagnosing, and records the decision

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare the room, yourself and the client before a seated head, neck and shoulder massage.
essays.modelAnswer: I prepare a warm, quiet, private area with soft lighting, fresh air and calm music. I wipe the chair with disinfectant and set out clean towels, a gown, tissues and the massage medium in a clean bowl, with a spatula for creams. I check the chair is steady. For myself, I tie back my hair, remove rings and watches, check my nails are short and clean, and wash my hands. I wear a clean uniform and flat shoes. For the client, I greet her and do a consultation, checking for contraindications and allergies, and she signs the consultation form. I ask her to remove earrings, necklaces and glasses, and to change into a gown or loosen her top if oil will be used, keeping her covered with a towel for warmth and modesty. I seat her upright, with her back supported, feet flat and arms relaxed, and explain what will happen.
markingPoints: Room: warm, quiet, private, soft lighting, clean chair and towels
Medium decanted into a clean bowl for this client
Therapist: hair tied back, no jewellery, short nails, hands washed
Consultation with contraindication and allergy check, signed form
Client: jewellery off, covered with a towel, seated upright and supported, told what will happen

essays.stem: Explain how you would put the massage movements together into a full routine, in order, from start to finish.
essays.modelAnswer: I begin with my hands resting lightly on the client's shoulders for a moment so she knows I am starting. I warm the medium in my hands and apply it with effleurage, long smooth strokes over the upper back, shoulders and neck, to spread it and warm the muscles. Next I use petrissage, kneading the tops of the shoulders and the trapezius, then the upper arms. I then use friction, small deep circles with my thumbs on either side of the spine and along the tops of the shoulder blades, to work on knots. I go back to effleurage to link the movements. I move to the neck, using gentle kneading and finger circles at the back, never on the throat. Then I massage the scalp with my finger pads in small circles, and finish with light stroking over the forehead and temples. I may use light tapotement on the shoulders. I end with slow effleurage and rest my hands still, then tell her quietly that the massage is finished.
markingPoints: Starts with contact and effleurage to spread the medium and warm the area
Petrissage on the shoulders, trapezius and upper arms
Friction on either side of the spine and around the shoulder blades
Neck and scalp worked gently, avoiding the throat
Links with effleurage and finishes slowly with effleurage and a still hold

essays.stem: Explain how you would adapt the massage for (a) a client with very tense shoulders, (b) an older client with thin skin, and (c) a client with braids or locs.
essays.modelAnswer: For the client with very tense shoulders, I would spend more time warming the area with effleurage before going deeper. I would then use slow petrissage and friction on the trapezius and around the shoulder blades, building up the pressure a little at a time and asking her how it feels. I would not press so hard that it hurts. For the older client with thin skin, I would use lighter pressure and more medium so that my hands glide without dragging the skin. I would avoid tapotement over bony areas and check that she is comfortable in the chair, especially her neck. For the client with braids or locs, I would ask whether she wants oil on her scalp. I would work with my finger pads between the braids or locs on the scalp, using small circles, and avoid pulling or rubbing the hair so that the braids are not loosened and the locs do not frizz.
markingPoints: Tense shoulders: longer warm-up, then build pressure slowly with petrissage and friction
Checks with the client and never presses so hard that it hurts
Thin skin: lighter pressure and more medium, no dragging
Older client: avoids tapotement over bone and checks neck comfort
Braids or locs: asks about oil, works with finger pads between them, no pulling or rubbing

essays.stem: Explain how to choose and use a massage medium (oil or cream) safely and hygienically.
essays.modelAnswer: At the consultation I ask about allergies, especially to nuts, because some oils are made from nuts, and I check the client's skin type. Oil suits dry skin and gives a good glide; cream suits normal skin and soaks in more; a client with very oily skin may need little or no medium. I read the label and follow the maker's instructions. If the client is unsure about a product, I do a small test on her skin first. I pour a small amount into a clean bowl for that client only, or take cream out with a clean spatula, and I never dip used fingers into the main bottle. I warm the medium in my hands before applying it, and use only enough for my hands to glide. Afterwards I wipe off any extra with a tissue, especially from the hairline and clothes. I close the bottle, store it in a cool, dark place and wash the bowl.
markingPoints: Asks about allergies, especially nut allergies, and checks skin type
Chooses a suitable medium for the skin, following the maker's instructions
Decants into a clean bowl or uses a spatula; never dips used fingers in the bottle
Warms it in the hands and uses only enough to glide
Wipes off extra, closes and stores the product safely, cleans the bowl

essays.stem: Describe the aftercare advice you would give after a massage. Name the mild reactions a client might feel and say what she should do.
essays.modelAnswer: After the massage I help the client sit up slowly and give her a glass of water. I advise her to drink plenty of water for the rest of the day, to rest if she can, and to avoid alcohol, heavy meals and hard exercise for a few hours. She should not do anything stressful straight away, and should avoid washing oil out of her hair with very hot water. I tell her that some mild reactions are normal and usually pass within a day: feeling tired or sleepy, a little light-headed, a mild headache, slight soreness in the muscles, needing to pass urine more often, or feeling emotional. She should rest and drink water if these happen. If a reaction is strong or lasts longer than a day or two, she should contact the salon and see a doctor. I record the advice on her record card and suggest when to book again.
markingPoints: Sits the client up slowly and gives water
Advises water, rest, and no alcohol, heavy meals or hard exercise for a while
Names at least three normal mild reactions
Tells her to rest and drink water, and to contact the salon or a doctor if a reaction is strong or lasts
Records the advice and suggests the next booking

essays.stem: Explain how a massage therapist should protect her own body during her working day.
essays.modelAnswer: A therapist uses her body all day, so she must work safely. She should adjust the client's chair so that she can work without bending or reaching too far. She stands with her feet apart, one slightly in front of the other, knees soft and back straight, and moves her feet to follow the strokes instead of twisting her back. She uses her body weight to give pressure, leaning in from the legs, and does not push with her thumbs alone, because this can hurt the thumb joints. She changes between thumbs, fingers, palms and the heels of her hands. She keeps her shoulders relaxed and down. Between clients she shakes out and stretches her hands, wrists and shoulders. She takes short breaks, drinks water and does not book too many massages in a row. She wears flat, comfortable shoes and looks after any cuts on her hands.
markingPoints: Adjusts the chair to avoid bending or reaching
Good stance: feet apart, knees soft, back straight, moves feet not back
Uses body weight and changes hand parts; does not overuse the thumbs
Stretches hands and shoulders between clients and takes breaks
Plans bookings sensibly and wears flat, comfortable shoes

essays.stem: Describe how you would carry out the consultation before a head, neck and shoulder massage. Say what you would ask, what you would look at and what you would record.
essays.modelAnswer: I take the client to a private area and explain what the massage involves and how long it takes. I ask why she wants the massage, for example stress or tight shoulders from work, and which areas bother her most. I ask about her general health: any medical conditions such as high or low blood pressure, heart problems, epilepsy or diabetes, recent injuries or operations, medicines she takes, and whether she might be pregnant. I ask about allergies, especially to nuts or perfumes, and whether she has eaten a heavy meal or drunk alcohol. I look at the skin of her neck and shoulders and her scalp for cuts, bruises, swelling, rashes or signs of infection. I ask what pressure she likes. I record her answers, any contraindications and what I decide, and she signs the form. If she needs a doctor's approval, I explain this kindly and rebook her.
markingPoints: Explains the treatment and asks the reason for the massage and problem areas
Asks about medical conditions, injuries, medicines and pregnancy
Asks about allergies, alcohol and heavy meals
Looks at the skin and scalp for contraindications and asks about pressure
Records answers and decisions, gets a signature, and refers kindly when needed

practical1.title: Full seated head, neck and shoulder massage with consultation
practical1.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5 in the Centre's treatment area. Each member gives a full seated head, neck and shoulder massage, lasting about 20 to 30 minutes, to a group partner who agrees. Before the massage, each therapist carries out a consultation, checks for contraindications and allergies, and the client signs the form. Use a medium only if the client has no allergies to it; otherwise massage dry, over a thin towel. Members take turns as therapist, client, timekeeper and photographer, so everyone does each job. The timekeeper notes the start and end times and the order of the movements. After the massage, the therapist gives aftercare advice and fills in the record card. Photograph only the shoulders, back of the head and the therapist's hands, never faces, unless the client agrees and the Centre allows it. Hand in once for the whole group with the photos, forms and timing notes.
materials: A sturdy chair with a back, or a massage chair
Clean towels and gowns for each client
Massage oil or cream with the maker's label, a clean bowl and a spatula for each client
Consultation and record forms, and pens
Disinfectant for surfaces and a laundry bin
photos: The treatment area set up, with the medium in a clean bowl
The signed consultation form (with personal details covered)
The client seated correctly and covered with a towel
Scalp massage with the finger pads
The area cleaned and towels in the laundry bin
checklist: Carried out a full consultation and checked for contraindications and allergies
Prepared the area, the medium and themselves hygienically
Positioned the client correctly, upright, supported and covered
Used effleurage, petrissage and friction correctly, in a sensible order
Kept the pressure suitable, checked with the client and avoided the spine and throat
Kept the movements smooth, rhythmic and continuous
Gave correct aftercare advice and completed the record card
Kept a good posture throughout and cleaned the area afterwards
safety: Do not massage any member who has a contraindication; tell the assessor
Ask about nut and other allergies before using any oil or cream
Never press on the spine or the front and sides of the neck
Stop if the client feels dizzy, unwell or in pain; keep her seated and give water
Help each client stand up slowly after the massage

practical2.title: Anatomy chart, contraindication checks and a dry massage over clothing
practical2.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5. Part 1: on A3 chart paper, draw an outline of the head, neck and shoulders from behind and from the side, and label the main bones and muscles. Each member labels at least two and explains them to the assessor. Part 2: the assessor gives each member a card describing a client, for example a client with whiplash, one with high blood pressure, one who has just eaten a big meal, one with a cut on her shoulder and one who is simply tired. Each member writes on a check sheet whether they would massage, adapt the massage or refer the client, and why. Part 3: each member gives a 15-minute dry massage, with no oil, over clothing, to a group partner seated in a chair, as might be offered at a workplace or event. Adapt the pressure to the partner. Photograph each part, showing only shoulders, backs of heads and hands, never faces. Hand in once for the whole group with the chart, the check sheets and the photos.
materials: A3 chart paper and coloured markers
A bones and muscles picture from the Centre's textbook, for checking
Client cards from the assessor and blank check sheets
A sturdy chair with a back, or a massage chair
photos: The A3 anatomy chart being labelled
The completed check sheets for the client cards
A partner seated correctly for the dry massage
checklist: Labelled bones and muscles correctly on the chart and explained them
Made the right decision for their client card: massage, adapt or refer
Gave a clear reason for the decision
Asked the partner about health and comfort before the massage
Used suitable movements over clothing, with pressure adapted to the partner
Avoided the spine and the front and sides of the neck
Kept a good posture and finished with aftercare advice
safety: Check each partner for contraindications before massaging; tell the assessor about any
No oil is used in Part 3; remove hard hair clips and jewellery first
Never press on the spine or the throat
Stop at once if the partner feels pain or dizziness
